Listen to this article Share Many Nigerians spend their days working and still struggle to cover their basic needs. Some combine several jobs. Others run small businesses that earn just enough to keep going, with little left to save or reinvest. For them, the problem is not a lack of effort. It is that effort alone does not translate into financial security. That is worth remembering whenever we talk about economic growth. Better national numbers matter, but people also need to feel progress in their own lives: income they can rely on, the ability to meet their responsibilities, and room to plan beyond the next bill. The World Bank’s April 2026 Nigeria Development Update points to this gap. It notes improvements in economic stability and public finances, while observing that household incomes have not fully recovered and poverty remains high. National progress, in other words, has not yet reached many homes. As a young professional, this is why the conversation about work matters to me. In my work with small business clients, and in my family’s building materials business, I see how much an owner’s month depends on things outside their control: the cost of power, a supplier who delivers late, customers who pay late. A good month does not necessarily mean a secure one. Growth should help businesses expand and open up opportunities that improve lives. So, we should ask not only how many people have work, but whether that work is productive enough to pay a living they can depend on. The National Bureau of Statistics reported unemployment of 4.3% in the second quarter of 2024. In the same period, 93% of employment was informal and 85.6% of employed people were self-employed. Most Nigerians, then, earn outside conventional salaried jobs. Self-employment is not the problem. Many good businesses begin with one person, a skill and a little capital. But being busy is not the same as being financially secure. Someone can work every day and still be unable to afford essentials or absorb a setback. So our ambition should go beyond getting people into any available activity. It should be work that gives a realistic chance of a better life. That starts with the businesses expected to create these jobs. Before hiring, a business owner must be confident they can bear the cost. Electricity, access to finance, transport and customer demand all shape that decision. When these pressures leave no room to grow, hiring stalls. Making it easier for businesses to operate is part of making better work available, and government support should be judged by whether firms are producing more, reaching more customers and keeping people employed. Preparing people for work calls for the same honesty. Training can help, but a certificate is not an income. A young person can finish a programme and still struggle to find an employer willing to take a chance. Employers and training providers should work together so that people learn skills businesses actually need. Paid apprenticeships and placements can bridge learning and earning, and these programmes should be judged by what follows: whether participants find work, stay employed or build businesses that support them. Entrepreneurship deserves the same realism. Encouraging someone to start a business is only the beginning. They may also need equipment, guidance on managing money, access to customers and finance they can realistically repay. We should be careful presenting this scenario as an easy answer to a shortage of jobs. The quality of existing jobs matters too. Clear terms, prompt pay, safe conditions and chances to learn all shape how people experience work. Employers have a part to play: as businesses grow, the people contributing to that growth should have their fair share. That is why we need a broader measure of progress. Employment figures help, but they do not tell the whole story. We should also ask whether earnings keep pace with living costs, whether jobs last, and whether more people are accessing better opportunities. The Work Nigeria sub-theme at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit is a chance to keep these questions at the centre of the growth agenda. Government, businesses and educational institutions should leave with practical commitments that tie economic progress to better livelihoods. Nigerians already put in considerable effort to keep themselves, their families and their businesses going. Growth should make it more possible for that effort to lead somewhere: a worker who can meet essential expenses and save, a business that can confidently employ one more person, a young graduate with a credible starting point. Those are the results that would make growth matter to the people doing the work. Ajibola is a Communications and Engagement Associate at Boucles Africa, a communications and public relations agency in Lagos, and a member of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group’s media and publicity sub-committee for the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit (NES#32).
